extracted.intended_audience: general readers; comedians, writers, and scholars interested in the nature and practice of dark/black comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing or producing comedy that treats taboo or serious subjects (especially death) with wit; covers definitions, functions, forms, and contextual constraints of dark/black/gallows humor. Useful for creators, critics, and students of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / core aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark humor is a style of comedy that makes light of subject matter that is generally considered taboo, particularly subjects that are normally considered serious or painful to discuss, aiming to provoke discomfort, serious thought, and amusement for their audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing dark humor, ensure the material treats taboo/serious topics (e.g., death, suffering) and intends a mix of discomfort, reflection, and amusement rather than pure shock or vulgarity. The interplay of those aims distinguishes dark humor from other types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary from blue comedy and obscenity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark humor differs from blue comedy — which focuses more on topics such as nudity, sex, and body fluids — and from obscenity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating dark humor with crude or sexual jokes; judge material by whether it engages taboo/serious themes and social commentary rather than merely using explicit sexual content or gratuitous obscenity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gallows humor specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Gallows humor tends to be used more specifically in relation to death, or situations that are reminiscent of dying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the material centers on death or imminent death, categorize it as gallows-style; evaluate whether its wit arises from confronting mortality (often producing a particular kind of stoic or bitter laughter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of wit: cynicism and skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit in (black) humor often arises from cynicism and skepticism, frequently relying on topics such as death (as noted by André Breton when coining 'humour noir').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the comedic stance is rooted in a skeptical/cynical view that reframes tragic or horrific realities into ironic or bitter commentary, rather than merely making light of suffering without an interrogative stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to the grotesque / genre overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark humor can occasionally be related to the grotesque genre and may employ grotesque satire to make the horror of an event perceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When grotesque elements are present (exaggeration, grotesque imagery), evaluate whether they serve to illuminate horror or merely to sensationalize; grotesque satire tends to 'add' elements and can intensify the painful aspects of the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is targeted / empathy vs. mockery
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two traditions: wit may arise from a victim with which the audience empathizes (typical gallows humor), or the comedy may be used to mock the victim; in the latter case the victim's suffering is trivialized, which leads to sympathizing with the victimizer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'punching up' (empathic, critical, subversive) from 'punching down' (mocking victims). Consider moral/ethical consequences: humor that trivializes suffering or encourages siding with the oppressor is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context sensitivity / teller identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'relieving' aspect of gallows jokes depends on the context of the joke: whether the joke is being told by the threatened person themselves or by someone else; outsiders may not react the way those with mutual knowledge do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate who is telling the joke and the shared knowledge/status between teller and audience. Jokes told by those experiencing the trauma (insider coping) are more likely to be relieving; the same joke told by an outsider can be interpreted as callous or offensive. Creators should note context for audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as coping mechanism in professions/environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Black comedy is common in professions and environments where workers routinely have to deal with dark subject matter (police, firefighters, ambulance crews, military, journalists, lawyers, funeral directors), where it is an acknowledged coping mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing such humor in professional contexts, weigh its role in morale, bonding, and emotional regulation for insiders. Document context and intended audience; recognize that professional use does not necessarily translate into acceptability for general audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of satire: ironic vs. grotesque (risata verde)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should distinguish satira ironica (ironic satire, works by subtraction) from satira grottesca (grotesque satire, works by addition) — the latter frequently generates the 'risata verde' (a laughter of despair) and can 'hurt' as well as amuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify a piece as ironic or grotesque satire and judge accordingly: ironic satire typically elicits laughter by understatement/subtraction, while grotesque/additive satire amplifies horrific elements to provoke a different, potentially painful laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/political effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Black comedy has the social effect of strengthening the morale of the oppressed and undermining the morale of the oppressors; it is used in social commentary and criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the humor targets powerful actors/institutions (potentially subversive/political) or merely exploits vulnerable people. Effective dark humor often functions as critique; ineffective or harmful examples may merely reinforce harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological/cognitive correlates (audience differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies suggest people who appreciate dark humor 'may have higher IQs, show lower aggression, and resist negative feelings more effectively' than those who dislike it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such findings cautiously: they describe audience variation rather than prescribe quality. When evaluating reception, consider that appreciation varies with cognitive/emotional traits and that offense or appreciation may reflect audience differences rather than intrinsic merit.
